query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: For an equiatomic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with an initially stable passive film, the tribo-corrosion response is governed by a dynamic equilibrium wherein mechanical wear repeatedly breaks the protective oxide layer, while rapid repassivation limits overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA with as-formed passive oxide film (via ambient exposure).
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled sliding in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution while comparing surfaces that are pre-passivated (via a short anodic polarization treatment) with mechanically polished surfaces.
generation.conditions: Room temperature, 3.5 wt% NaCl environment, sliding load and speed chosen to induce partial film rupture without complete mechanical failure.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and continuity of the passive oxide film (comprising oxides such as Cr2O3 or mixed spinels).
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear locally ruptures the passive film, exposing fresh material to aggressive chemical attack; rapid repassivation reforms the protective film, leading to a dynamic balance that governs overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with an artificially stabilized passive film will exhibit approximately 30–50% lower total degradation, reduced corrosion pit density, and smoother OCP profiles compared to unmodified (baseline) samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA samples with their naturally formed passive film.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold under moderate mechanical loads where the film can periodically reform; it would likely fail under extreme loads leading to complete film removal.
generation.uncertainty: Variability in repassivation kinetics and local chemical heterogeneity may affect the magnitude of the observed improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi samples: one set undergoes a pre-passivation treatment (e.g., brief controlled anodic polarization) and the other remains mechanically polished. Conduct identical tribo-corrosion tests (sliding in 3.5 wt% NaCl) with real-time monitoring of OCP and friction coefficient, complemented by post-test weight loss and localized pit analysis.
measurements: Wear track morphology and pit density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-passivated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction (e.g., ~30–50% lower degradation) in wear and corrosion indicators compared to the baseline, or if the OCP profiles remain similarly unstable, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Tribocorrosion Performance after Annealing in Air Environment
cited_evidence.text: The influence of thermal shock on the tribocorrosion properties of AlCrTiZrMo HEA films is analyzed by monitoring the fluctuation of the OCP and COF of films in the coupled environment of friction and corrosion, as shown in Figure 10. The fluctuation of the OCP and COF of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C for 1 h in air are monitored in real time. In the preparation stage, the samples were completely immersed in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution for 1 h to obtain a stable surface potential. The duration of the whole experiment is 50 min. During the no-load phase of 0–10 min, both the OCP and COF curves remain stable. During the 10–40 min loading stage, the appearance of the activation region causes the OCP curve to drop sharply, then fluctuate around a constant value. During the 40–50 min no-loading stage, the lack of load causes re-passivation within the wear track, and the OCP curve gradually returns to stability. Therefore, OCP can be used as a mixed potential to monitor the passivation state within the wear track [,,].

The passive oxide-layer on the surface of SS-304 may become compromised at high temperatures and in the presence of chloride-ions. This may result in homogenously corrosion, in which the surface corrodes uniformly throughout. cited_evidence.text: The cathodic line shifts from A2 to A3, causing point C to move towards point D. In stage (4), the continuous growth of the passive film on the sample surface consumes oxygen in the solution, thereby reducing the cathodic reaction rate. The cathodic line moves from A3 to A4, causing point D to move towards point E. Additionally, with prolonged exposure to CE, the transition from point B to point C tends to follow a linear trend. This is attributed to the increasing cumulative damage on the sample surface with extended CE time, leading to localized rupture and repassivation of the passive film, and eventually reaching a balance of dynamic equilibrium.

papers.title: Investigation of surface hardness, thermostability, tribo-corrosion, and microstructural morphological properties of microwave-synthesized high entrop
papers.system: SS-304 steel coated with a microwave-synthesized Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 high-entropy alloy (HEA)
papers.approach: Microwave cladding and post-thermal exposure in air at high temperatures; evaluation of corrosion behavior through surface morphology, oxide formation and wear behavior under combined friction-corrosion conditions.
papers.findings: The HEA coating formed protective oxide scales (e.g., Cr2O3 and spinel oxides) that reduced corrosion loss and enhanced wear resistance under high-temperature and chloride-ion exposure. However, localized breakdown (pitting) occurred where the passive film was compromised.
papers.mechanism: A key mechanism is the formation of a continuous, protective oxide (passive) layer that mitigates both uniform corrosion and wear; mechanical stresses during sliding rupture this film locally, exposing the substrate to corrosion followed by repassivation.

papers.title: Study on cavitation erosion-corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high entropy alloy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high-entropy alloy in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution
papers.approach: Electrochemical testing (OCP monitoring, potentiodynamic polarization, and noise analysis) under alternating cavitation erosion (CE) and quiescent conditions to disentangle the contributions from mechanical damage and corrosion.
papers.findings: The study quantified that nearly 48% of the cumulative mass loss is due to the synergistic effect between mechanical CE damage and corrosion. The passive film on the alloy was shown to play a critical role, with its rupture and subsequent repassivation dictating the transition between active corrosion and protection.
papers.mechanism: The synergism arises from CE-induced removal of the passive film, which accelerates corrosion processes; upon quiescence, repassivation reduces the corrosion rate, indicating that the dynamic balance between film rupture and repair governs the degradation.

papers.title: Self-Lubricating Tribo-Catalytic Activity of 2D High Entropy Alloy Nanoflakes.
papers.approach: Ball-on-disk tribological experiments combined with molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate friction and wear under high contact pressures in ambient conditions.
papers.findings: The 2D HEA exhibited extremely low friction coefficients and wear rates. The study revealed that under shear, tribocatalytic reactions promote energy dissipation and formation of a lubricious surface layer that prolongs lubricant life.
papers.mechanism: The mechanism is attributed to stress‐induced energy dissipation through shear‐triggered tribocatalytic activity, which effectively contributes to forming a self-lubricating film.

papers.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMoTi HEA coatings with varied boron (B) content fabricated on Q235 steel
papers.approach: Laser cladding with controlled B microalloying; characterization via SEM, EIS, potentiodynamic polarization, and wear tests to examine the influence of B on phase stability, passive film formation, and wear mechanisms.
papers.findings: A small addition of B (e.g., x = 0.5) enhanced the passive film's stability and improved corrosion resistance, while too high B content led to agglomerated TiB2 particles that compromised the film integrity, increasing wear and corrosion rates.
papers.mechanism: Boron triggers in situ formation of TiB2 and refines the BCC phase structure, which improves both microhardness and the formation/stability of the protective passive layer. However, excessive boron results in defects that reduce the self-healing ability of the passive film, indicating a balance between film robustness and particle-induced damage.

papers.title: Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film.
papers.system: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy films produced by cathode vacuum arc deposition
papers.approach: Thermal annealing at various temperatures (400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C) in air combined with tribocorrosion experiments monitored via OCP and friction coefficient measurements, along with cross-sectional and surface analyses.
papers.findings: Annealing at 800 °C resulted in the formation of a dense composite oxide layer (e.g., ZrTiO4) that enhanced tribocorrosion resistance by stabilizing the surface under combined friction and corrosion environments, with the lowest fluctuations in OCP, COF, and wear rate observed.
papers.mechanism: The improved performance is linked to the formation of a stable, dense oxide layer during thermal shock, which acts as a self-healing passive film. The dynamic balance between wear-induced disruption of the film and its repassivation stabilizes the tribocorrosion response.

papers.title: Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA fabricated via additive manufacturing
papers.approach: Sliding contact experiments performed in ultra-high vacuum (UHV) combined with microstructural analysis (STEM) and an amorphization model to correlate grain size with friction behavior.
papers.findings: It was observed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable in the absence of oxidation, being linked to shear-induced dynamic grain refinement (inverse Hall-Petch behavior) and the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
papers.mechanism: The mechanism is based on dynamic amorphization, where wear-induced grain refinement reduces surface shear strength. Although this study was conducted in inert environments, it contributes a perspective on how microstructural evolution under shear could interplay with passive film dynamics in corrosive conditions.

papers.title: Effect of Grain Size on the Tribological Behavior of CoCrFeMnNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: CoCrFeMnNi HEAs with varying grain sizes (fine-grained and coarse-grained)
papers.approach: Systematic sliding experiments under varied normal loads and sliding speeds; worn surface morphology and element analysis to determine wear mechanisms (adhesive, oxidative, plastic deformation).
papers.findings: Fine-grained samples exhibited lower friction coefficients and better wear resistance due to the formation of more stable oxide layers and higher surface strength, whereas coarse-grained samples showed more pronounced oxidative wear and plastic deformation under similar conditions.
papers.mechanism: Grain size influences the capacity of the material to form and retain a protective oxide layer during tribological loading. The dynamic rupture and repair of this passive film under different mechanical loads govern the overall tribocorrosion behavior.

established: Protective passive oxide films play a critical role in mitigating corrosion in HEAs, and their formation is sensitive to alloy composition and environmental conditions.
Mechanical wear can disrupt these passive films, initiating localized corrosion which, upon repassivation, governs the overall degradation.
Tribocorrosion in HEAs is governed by the interplay between mechanical stresses (e.g., sliding wear) and chemical processes (e.g., passive film breakdown and formation).

approaches_tried.approach: Microwave cladding and thermal treatment to form protective oxide layers
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced corrosion and wear resistance through stable oxide (passive layer) formation, though with localized pitting when the film is breached.

approaches_tried.approach: Electrochemical evaluation under cavitation erosion (CE) conditions
approaches_tried.outcome: Quantified the synergistic loss due to CE-induced passive film rupture and subsequent corrosion, confirming the importance of dynamic repassivation.
Optimized balance between phase formation and passive film stability to maximize both wear and corrosion resistance.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal shock and annealing of amorphous HEA films
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that high-temperature annealing leads to the formation of a dense, protective oxide layer that stabilizes tribocorrosion behavior.

mechanisms: Dynamic equilibrium between mechanical removal (due to wear) of the passive oxide film and its repassivation
Stress-induced tribocatalytic activity that contributes to in situ formation of lubricious surface layers
Grain refinement (inverse Hall-Petch behavior) altering surface shear strength and affecting film stability
disagreements: Some studies report that oxide formation during sliding can act lubriciously to reduce friction, whereas others emphasize that film rupture increases localized corrosion and wear.
Differences in environmental conditions (e.g., UHV versus corrosive solutions) lead to contrasting conclusions on the dominance of tribocorrosion mechanisms.
open_questions: How do variations in microstructural features (e.g., grain size, phase distribution) quantitatively affect the balance between passive film rupture and repassivation during tribo-corrosion?
What is the precise role of alloying additions (such as B) in modulating the integrity and self-healing ability of passive films under combined mechanical and chemical attack?
Under what specific environmental and loading conditions does one mechanism (film rupture/repassivation versus tribocatalytic lubrication) become dominant?
opportunities: Conduct controlled comparisons by pre-forming stable passive films versus mechanically pre-damaged surfaces to isolate the impact of film integrity on tribocorrosion behavior.

Combine systematic variation of sliding load, speed, and environmental factors (e.g., chloride concentration, temperature) with real-time electrochemical monitoring to directly correlate passive film evolution with degradation rates.
Explore the integration of microalloying strategies (e.g., boron addition) with grain size engineering to simultaneously optimize both wear resistance and corrosion protection in HEAs.

Utilize in situ observation techniques (e.g., real-time OCP and friction measurement) to quantifiably test the hypothesis of dynamic film rupture and repassivation as the governing mechanism, where a failure to observe reduced degradation with artificially stabilized passive layers would falsify the hypothesis.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of a dynamic equilibrium between passive film rupture (due to mechanical wear) and repassivation (due to chemical exposure) in governing the overall tribo-corrosion response.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the primary limitation by linking mechanical disruption and corrosion protection. The underlying physics of film rupture and reformation are well supported by evidence, and controlled electrochemical plus mechanical testing is feasible and highly informative.

directions.direction: Examine how grain size engineering and the associated dynamic amorphization (inverse Hall‐Petch effect) modify the stability of the passive film during tribo-corrosion.
directions.assessment: Attacks the coupled wear-corrosion mechanism by correlating microstructural refinement with enhanced film homogeneity and repassivation kinetics. Both simulation and controlled experiments comparing fine versus coarse grains are supported by available evidence.

directions.direction: Utilize microalloying (e.g., boron addition) to tailor the phase formation (via in situ TiB2 formation) and passive film stability to modulate the tribo-corrosion response.
directions.assessment: Directly alters the degradation behavior through compositional tuning that influences oxide film formation. Prior studies show promising results with optimal B content; the approach is feasible via laser cladding with careful control of alloy chemistry.

directions.direction: Induce a controlled thermal shock (annealing) to form a dense composite oxide (e.g., ZrTiO4) that acts as a self-healing passive film during tribo-corrosion.
directions.assessment: Uses thermal processing to pre-form a stable, continuous oxide layer, directly addressing the passive film breakdown under combined wear and corrosion. The mechanism is supported by evidence from thermal shock studies, although it is sensitive to environmental conditions.

directions.direction: Probe the contribution of stress‐induced tribocatalytic reactions and shear‐triggered lubricious film formation in reducing degradation under tribocorrosion.
directions.assessment: Focuses on an alternative mechanism where in situ formation of a self-lubricating layer affects friction and wear. While innovative, the dependence on ambient conditions and contrasting evidence makes it a less universally applicable explanation for coupled degradation.

candidates.hypothesis: Incorporating trace amounts of boron into an AlCoCrFeNiMoTi HEA coating improves tribo-corrosion resistance by promoting the in situ formation of finely dispersed TiB2 particles, which refine the microstructure and help stabilize the passive film against mechanical rupture.

candidates.hypothesis: Thermal shock annealing of amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA films at high temperatures (800 °C for 1 hour) induces the formation of a dense composite oxide (predominantly ZrTiO4) that serves as a self-healing passive film, thereby moderating the tribo-corrosion response under simultaneous mechanical sliding and corrosive attack.
candidates.intervention: Subject the films to a thermal shock annealing treatment at 800 °C for 1 hour in ambient air to promote the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer.
